extracted.intended_audience: toxicologists, risk assessors, regulators, emergency planners (EPA, DOD, ATSDR), and reviewers of AEGL reports
extracted.subtask_description: Development and independent review of Acute Exposure Guideline Levels (AEGLs) for airborne chemicals, including data collection, hazard evaluation, dose extrapolation, uncertainty assessment, and procedural steps for drafting, public comment, and NRC review.

rubrics_metrics.name: AEGL level definitions (AEGL-1, AEGL-2, AEGL-3)
rubrics_metrics.description: AEGL-1, AEGL-2, and AEGL-3 are three levels developed for each exposure period and are defined by degrees of severity of toxic effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AEGL-1: airborne concentration above which the general population, including susceptible individuals, could experience notable discomfort, irritation, or certain asymptomatic nonsensory effects; effects are not disabling and are transient and reversible upon cessation of exposure. AEGL-2: airborne concentration above which the general population, including susceptible individuals, could experience irreversible or other serious, long-lasting adverse health effects or an impaired ability to escape. AEGL-3: airborne concentration above which the general population, including susceptible individuals, could experience life-threatening adverse health effects or death. Concentrations are expressed as ppm or mg/m3. With increasing airborne concentrations above each AEGL there is a progressive increase in the likelihood and severity of effects described for that AEGL.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposure durations and averaging periods
rubrics_metrics.description: AEGL values are applicable to emergency exposures ranging from 10 minutes to 8 hours and are developed for five exposure periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AEGLs are specified for 10 min, 30 min, 1 h, 4 h, and 8 h. Select the AEGL corresponding to the appropriate exposure duration for planning and response scenarios; recognize that duration influences dose-response and extrapolation assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of evidence to collect and review
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect and review all relevant published and unpublished information from multiple evidence streams to establish AEGLs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence includes (1) chemical–physical characterizations, (2) structure–activity relationships, (3) in vitro toxicity studies, (4) animal toxicity studies, (5) controlled human studies, (6) observations of humans involved in chemical accidents, and (7) epidemiologic studies. Toxicity data from human studies are most applicable and are preferred when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for inhalation and human data; route relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize inhalation toxicity data and human studies when setting AEGLs because inhalation is the most likely route for airborne chemicals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use human inhalation data in preference to animal or non-inhalation data. Extrapolating from other exposure routes adds uncertainty and should be done cautiously; explicitly document and justify additional uncertainty when non-inhalation data are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interspecies extrapolation and choice of animal data
rubrics_metrics.description: When human data are lacking, extrapolate animal data to humans using scientific judgment about species representativeness and sensitivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use data from the animal species most representative of humans in pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic properties; if unavailable, use data from the most sensitive species. Consider pharmacokinetic tissue-dose data when available to inform interspecies extrapolation and reduce uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and magnitude of uncertainty factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply uncertainty factors when extrapolating animal data to humans and when data gaps exist; the magnitude of factors depends on data quality and mode of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uncertainty factors are commonly used to account for interspecies differences, intraspecies variability, and data deficiencies. The size of the factor(s) depends on the quality of the animal data used to determine the NOAEL (no-observed-adverse-effect level) and on knowledge of the substance's mode of action; justify the choice and magnitude of each uncertainty factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration and prioritization of toxicological endpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate all relevant end points (reproductive, developmental, neurotoxic, respiratory, other organ-related effects) for substances that affect multiple systems and focus on the most sensitive or important effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When multiple end points are affected, give greatest attention to the most important or most sensitive end point in deriving AEGLs. Explicitly present and justify the selected critical end point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of carcinogens (excess risk estimation)
rubrics_metrics.description: For carcinogenic chemicals, estimate excess carcinogenic risk and derive AEGLs corresponding to specified excess-risk levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate AEGLs corresponding to excess carcinogenic risks of 1 in 10,000 (1 × 10−4), 1 in 100,000 (1 × 10−5), and 1 in 1,000,000 (1 × 10−6) exposed persons, and document methods and assumptions used in the cancer-risk extrapolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of susceptible subpopulations
rubrics_metrics.description: AEGLs are intended to be protective of the general public, including susceptible individuals such as infants, children, the elderly, and persons with diseases (e.g., asthma, heart disease).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop AEGLs recognizing susceptible subpopulations; note that idiosyncratic individual responses could occur below AEGL values. Explicitly consider sensitive groups in uncertainty factors and end-point selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural requirements for AEGL document development and review
rubrics_metrics.description: AEGL documents follow a structured development and review process involving ad hoc development teams, NAC review, public comment, and NRC committee evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drafts are prepared by AEGL development teams (chemical manager, two chemical reviewers, staff scientist), reviewed by NAC and elevated from draft to proposed, published in the Federal Register for public comment, revised by NAC to interim status, and finally sent to the NRC Committee on Acute Exposure Guideline Levels for independent evaluation. NRC review involves oral and written presentations, iterative revisions, and advice to ensure scientific validity and consistency with NRC guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and limits of NRC review responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The NRC committee evaluates scientific validity and consistency with guideline reports but cannot verify every data point in AEGL reports and relies on NAC for data accuracy and completeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that NRC's role is independent evaluation for validity and consistency rather than exhaustive data verification; significant data gaps or errors should be flagged, but the committee depends on NAC for the underlying data compilation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation, transparency, and public comment
rubrics_metrics.description: AEGL reports must be documented clearly and undergo public comment via Federal Register publication as part of the accepted process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide thorough documentation of data sources, rationale for critical end-point selection, uncertainty factors, extrapolation methods, and revisions in response to public comment. Ensure transparency to support independent review and stakeholder input.
